longQuestions: Population — the whole collection of individuals or items under study (all students of a college).
Sample — a part of the population selected to represent it (100 students).
Sampling — the process of selecting a sample from a population in order to draw conclusions about the population.

Sampling is needed because it saves time, money and labour; gives results quickly; makes more detailed and accurate study possible with trained staff; is the only method when the population is infinite or when testing destroys items (life of bulbs); and when the population is scattered or not fully accessible. Complete enumeration (census) is costly, slow and sometimes impossible.
(i) Sampling frame — a complete list of all units of the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g. voters' list).
(ii) Sample design — the plan for selecting the sample: the method of selection, sample size and estimation procedure.
(iii) Survey — a method of collecting information from a population or sample, by census or sample survey, through questionnaires, interviews or observation.
(i) A finite population has a fixed, countable number of units (students of a class); an infinite population has an unlimited number (stars, tosses of a coin).

(ii) In sampling with replacement each selected unit is returned before the next draw, so a unit can be selected more than once and draws are independent; without replacement a unit can appear only once and draws are dependent.

(iii) Sampling error is the difference between a sample estimate and the population parameter due to studying only a part of the population; non-sampling errors arise from mistakes in collection, recording, processing, non-response or bias and occur in both census and samples.

(a) Objectives of sampling: to obtain information about the population at less cost and time; to estimate population parameters; to test hypotheses about the population; and to measure the reliability of estimates.

(b) Parameter — a numerical value describing the population (μ, σ, P); statistic — a value computed from a sample (x̄, s, p̂); estimator — a statistic (rule/formula) used to estimate a parameter, e.g. x̄ for μ.
Sampling errors arise because only a part of the population is studied; they can be reduced by increasing the sample size and using better (e.g. stratified) sampling designs.

Non-sampling errors arise from faulty questionnaires, wrong or missing responses, interviewer bias, recording and processing mistakes; they are reduced by careful planning, training of staff, pre-testing questionnaires, follow-up of non-respondents and careful checking of data.

Probability (random) sampling: every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection; selection is by chance; results can be generalised and sampling error measured (simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster sampling).

Non-probability sampling: selection depends on the judgement or convenience of the investigator; chances are unknown; results may be biased and error cannot be measured (purposive, quota, convenience sampling).
(i) Simple random sampling — every unit (and every sample of size n) has an equal chance of selection, using lottery or random number tables.
(ii) Stratified random sampling — the population is divided into homogeneous groups (strata) and a random sample is taken from each stratum, often in proportion to its size.
(iii) Systematic random sampling — units are arranged in order; the first unit is selected at random from the first k units (k = N/n) and then every kth unit is taken.
A simple random sample is one in which every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
(i) Goldfish bowl (lottery) method: write the number of each unit on identical slips, put them in a bowl, mix thoroughly and draw n slips one by one.

(ii) Random number table method: number the units, read numbers of the required digits from a random number table, and select the units whose numbers appear, ignoring numbers outside the range and repeats (without replacement).
(i) Random sample — every unit has a known (equal) chance of selection.
(ii) Non-random sample — units are chosen by judgement or convenience, not by chance.
(iii) Stratified random sample — random samples taken from each homogeneous sub-group (stratum) of the population.
(iv) Systematic random sample — every kth unit taken after a random start.
Number the cities 001 to 200.
From any random starting point in the random number table read three-digit numbers; select a city if its number is between 001 and 200, skipping larger numbers and repeats.
Example (random start, reading down a column): 128, 057, 193, 004, 162, 079, 145, 031, 110, 186 → these 10 cities form the sample. (The actual numbers depend on the table used.)

longQuestions: (i) Sampling distribution — the probability distribution of a statistic (e.g. x̄) obtained from all possible samples of the same size from a population.
(ii) Standard error — the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic, e.g. σ_x̄ = σ/√n.
(iii) Finite population correction (fpc) — the factor √[(N − n)/(N − 1)] used in the standard error when sampling without replacement from a finite population; it is ignored when n < 5% of N.
The sampling distribution of x̄₁ − x̄₂ is the distribution of the differences of means of all possible pairs of independent samples of sizes n₁ and n₂ from two populations.
Properties: mean μ_{x̄₁−x̄₂} = μ₁ − μ₂; standard error σ_{x̄₁−x̄₂} = √(σ₁²/n₁ + σ₂²/n₂); it is normal if the populations are normal and approximately normal for large samples.
Sample proportion p̂ = X/n, the fraction of units in a sample having a characteristic.

The sampling distribution of p̂ is its distribution over all possible samples of size n. Properties: mean μ_p̂ = P; standard error σ_p̂ = √(PQ/n) (with fpc √[(N−n)/(N−1)] for finite populations without replacement); approximately normal for large n.
